benchmark_notes: The protocol derives its flat scale from the PCA flop count N d min(N, d). That is NOT where the time goes at the production size: compute_predictions (the d x d eigendecomposition of K plus the QR of the direction frame) is comparable to or larger than the SVD, and at the fixture size both are dwarfed by Python overhead.

Both production sizes (d = 256 with N = 128 and with N = 1024) were run directly, in BOTH geometry arms (correlated and orthogonal), so every one of the eight data families is a MEASUREMENT of its own configuration.

cpu_seconds.excludes: transfer and environment setup, which are reported separately below.  Per-worker interpreter start-up is NOT in the per-cell figures either: it is measured (0.106 s per worker process) and reported under 'harness_work.per_worker_interpreter_startup_seconds_measured', and it is not added to the total because how often a worker process starts is a property of the scheduler, which is unknown.
cpu_seconds.harness_is: the per-cell cost of this CLI around the kernel - ledger start/complete under the advisory flock, the schema and fit-accounting checks and the atomic result write (json encode + fsync + sha256) - measured end to end and priced per production cell.  The kernel benchmarks do not see it.

cross_check_flat_fixture_scale.compared_with: cpu_seconds.total_point, i.e. cell compute + the per-cell CLI harness + the reduction.  The flat product estimated a whole run, so a whole run is what it must be compared with; the ratio against cell compute alone is given separately and is not the correction.
cross_check_flat_fixture_scale.verdict: the declared flat scale disagrees with the measured TOTAL by a factor 60.2; the flat factor is wrong, not the measurement
cross_check_flat_fixture_scale.what_this_is: NOT the estimate.  One fixture wall time per family multiplied by the constant budget.fixture_to_production_scale, i.e. a flat linear extrapolation of the fixture with no dimension and no algorithmic scaling in it.  Kept so that the size of its error against the measurement is visible.

estimate_basis: measured benchmarks of the package's own kernels at four or more problem sizes that bracket or reach the production dimension, fitted as t = a n^b and reported beside the algorithm's exponent, multiplied by the enumerated production matrix.  NOT a fixture time multiplied by a declared constant; that product is kept separately under 'cross_check_flat_fixture_scale' and is not the estimate.

algebraic.how: the three algebraic cells are two geometry-invariant checks (0.0034 s each) and one predictor sanity check (0.0032 s); the family mean is their average

harness_work.per_worker_interpreter_startup_note: the interpreter start-up and package import above is paid once per worker PROCESS, not once per cell; a scheduler that starts a fresh process per cell pays it on every cell instead, which would add 0.106 s x 2499 cells = 265 CPU-s
harness_work.serial_note: ledger start+complete run under an advisory flock on one lock file, so they do not parallelise: this is a floor on the wall time that no worker count beats

parallelism_assumption: Cells are independent processes, so the cell compute and the parallel part of the per-cell harness are taken as perfectly parallel over W workers.  Two terms are NOT parallel and are added whole: the ledger appends, which every worker serialises through one advisory flock, and the reduction, which is a single process.  wall = (cell_compute + parallel_harness) / W + serial_ledger + reduction.  The serial ledger term is a floor no worker count beats.

peak_memory.per_cell_peak_chosen_by: the largest fresh-subprocess RSS measurement among the kernels, because only a fresh process attributes the high-water mark to one cell; in-process points are listed in all_points and are upper bounds on the whole benchmark process, not on one cell
peak_memory.per_worker_note: one worker holds one cell, so W workers need about W x the RSS figure above; this machine has 7 GiB, the server's memory is UNKNOWN
peak_memory.rss_is: VmHWM (resident high-water mark) of the process running the cell, including the interpreter and numpy; measured in a fresh subprocess where 'measured_in' says 'subprocess', which is the only way the high-water mark belongs to one problem size.  VmHWM and not ru_maxrss: Linux inherits ru_maxrss across fork, so a probe spawned by a benchmark driver reports the driver's peak, not the child's
peak_memory.tracemalloc_is: peak Python-allocator bytes attributable to the call

per_cell_central_statistic: seconds_per_cell_median is the measured median over repeats where the family's cells are identical, and the mean over the family's own cells of their measured medians where they are not (t20s N grid, cresst_s constructions / reports / ranks / designs, t22s n_files census).  The low/high bounds are the corresponding measured minima and maxima; they are measurements, not margins.
priced_cells_note: the total covers exactly the cells in 'priced_counts': the production matrix with role 'development' (fixture-only work, never transferred) excluded

production_projection.key_name_note: this block prices CELL COMPUTE only; the file's top-level 'total_cpu_seconds_point' is cell compute + harness + reduction.  The two are deliberately named differently so they cannot be read as the same number.
production_projection.note: per-cell seconds are MEASURED at the production dimension (d = 256 with N = 128 and with N = 1024 were both run directly), not a fixture time times a declared scale; the reduce cost is listed separately because the per-cell figures exclude it

1.conditional: CONDITIONAL on the server having 1 usable cores at a per-core speed comparable to the benchmark Xeon.  The server specification is NOT known; this is not a claim that 1 cores exist.

32.conditional: CONDITIONAL on the server having 32 usable cores at a per-core speed comparable to the benchmark Xeon.  The server specification is NOT known; this is not a claim that 32 cores exist.

8.conditional: CONDITIONAL on the server having 8 usable cores at a per-core speed comparable to the benchmark Xeon.  The server specification is NOT known; this is not a claim that 8 cores exist.

at_production_scale.note: At the production scale reduce reads 6 MB in 3.63 s, i.e. 1.7 MB/s, still far below the 50 MB/s at which I/O would take over, so the compute-bound classification measured on the fixture also holds at production for this package.

reduction_work.basis: projected from a measured per-cell rate
reduction_work.bound_note: reduce reads every cell file once; measured throughput 3.7 MB/s over 419 cells (2.33 MB of input) against a warm page cache, so the step is compute-bound AT THAT SIZE.  This is not a claim about the production scale; see reduction_work.at_production_scale in RESOURCE_ESTIMATE.json
reduction_work.how: measured seconds per cell on the fixture run root (419 cells) x the production cell count; linear because reduce reads each cell file exactly once

reduces_priced.what: final reduce over the whole run root

retry_allowance.cpu_seconds_per_retried_cell: the family's seconds_per_cell above; a retry costs a whole cell and is charged at start
retry_allowance.policy: one retry per failed cell, charged; a second failure of the same cell stops the run for inspection; headroom under the cap = 254 fits (10.2% of the plan); failures, retries and interrupts are never refunded

requirements.pip_dry_run_note: a real `pip install` of these pins was NOT timed: this container already satisfies them and has no guaranteed network egress, so the honest figure is the check time above. On a remote host without them, budget the download of numpy+scipy wheels (~90 MB) plus install, which is link-dependent and UNKNOWN.

transfer.note: the wall time of the transfer depends on the link, which is UNKNOWN; only the size is a fact. Measured on a build of this handoff; successive builds differ by a few tens of kB (timestamps, this report and the estimate files) - two builds of the same tree measured here were 7 702 123 and 7 764 484 bytes.

unknowns: server core count (the wall-time rows are conditional on 1, 8 and 32; none of them is asserted)
server per-core speed relative to the benchmark Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz
server BLAS threading policy (these numbers are single-threaded; a multithreaded BLAS changes the per-cell time and the useful worker count in opposite directions)
server filesystem speed and whether advisory flock on the ledger works there (a network filesystem falls back to serial ledger appends, which caps useful parallelism)
link bandwidth for the transfer (only the archive size is known)
whether the pinned requirements are already installed on the server
server memory per worker (the per-cell RSS figures above are measured; the budget is not known)

contention between concurrent workers: every per-cell time here was measured on a 2-vCPU container running ONE process at a time, so the numbers contain no cache, memory-bandwidth or disk contention. W concurrent workers share last-level cache, memory bandwidth and one disk queue, which makes each cell slower by an amount this benchmark cannot see and which grows with W.  The wall-time rows at 8 and 32 workers are therefore optimistic by an unmeasured factor.
